doc.title: Steve Allen interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 15, 1999

title: Golden Age American songs played in a Moscow hotel dining room
summary: Allen describes growing up in the Golden Age of American music and hearing a small band play Berlin, Gershwin and Kern at the Ukraina Hotel in 1958.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Yeah, there were probably three loose edge stages, counting for the development of my musical tastes and preferences. The first factor is that I was very lucky, given that I would eventually be a composer, a very busy one, even to the present moment, because I grew up in the true Golden Age of American music, and in fact world music. I don’t know how many Americans know this and of those who know it I don’t know how many care, but in that Golden Age you heard the best American music, all the Gershwin, Kern, Duke Ellington, Hoagy Carmichael stuff, all over the world. To take a specific date, in 1958 my wife and I were in the Soviet Union for about a two week study trip, and we were put up in Moscow at the Ukraina Hotel, an enormous and rather ugly establishment. But anyway we went down to the dining room for the first day’s dinner and all we were interested in was food, but as I got near the entrance to the room I was pleased to hear music. I thought oh, a nice extra plus. I wasn’t even counting on this. And then as I got still closer I realized they were playing American music. Now it wasn’t to welcome us, they didn’t know who I was, and there were probably 800 people in the dining room at the moment so they couldn’t be playing Philippine music for Filipinos, and American music for — that was out. But what they were doing for the next hour or so, a little six or seven piece © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -2-

group, they weren’t playing jazz, although one guy was almost in the jazz area, they were just playing songs that they obviously loved to play. And the great majority of them, and this was at the height of the Cold War, when American culture in general was more or less spat upon by the officials there. Nevertheless these guys were playing Golden Age stuff: Irving Berlin songs and George Gershwin songs and Jerome Kern songs. So I had a big smile on my face all through dinner. The food itself wasn’t that great.
Maybe the music was a distraction.
You can almost bet that they learned those songs off black market recordings, too.
That the sheet music wouldn’t be available.
